newsitem.title: GERMANY: German GDP data leaves goals hard to reach.
newsitem.headline: German GDP data leaves goals hard to reach.

text.p: Germany's economy grew by only 1.4 percent in the first quarter, the government said Thursday, raising more questions over whether Bonn can qualify for the single European currency.
When corrected for seasonal factors, however, Germany's gross domestic product grew a more encouraging 2.8 percent from the same quarter last year, the Federal Statistics Office said.
Still, the figures cast doubt on whether the government could reach its target of 2.5 percent growth this year.

They suggested little relief for Germany's towering unemployment rate, the cost of which is a major problem as Bonn desperately tries to cut its budget deficit to qualify for European economic and monetary union.

Most private sector economists appeared to accept the higher of the growth figures as giving a more accurate picture of the economy. But they still took it with a grain of salt and said Bonn would have a hard time reaching its target of 2.5 percent growth for the full year.
"The calendar factors won't necessarily be made up in the rest of the year," said economist Holger Fahrinkrug at UBS in Frankfurt.
An early Easter meant there were three fewer workdays in the first quarter this year, shaving more than a full percentage point off the economic growth rate, the Statistics Office said.
German hopes of qualifying for economic and monetary union ride on the GDP goal because sluggish growth and continued high unemployment hamper efforts to trim the budget deficit to target levels.
Finance Minister Theo Waigel has repeatedly said Germany will be able to meet its goals, but he bases that forecast on the economy growing by 2.5 percent.
